title: Mass Extinctions
objective: After this level you can explain the five mass extinctions, including the asteroid that ended the dinosaurs.
summary: Five mass extinctions stand out; the end-Permian was worst. The end-Cretaceous one, 66 million years ago, is best explained by the Chicxulub asteroid.

cards.headline: Nearly every species that has ever lived is extinct.
cards.body: Species come and go all the time. But five times, the fossil record shows the dying on a planetary scale. The most famous ended 66 million years ago, with a rock from space. How do we know that one really happened?

events.label: End-Permian: the worst, about 90 percent of species

cards.headline: The clue in the clay
cards.body: In 1980, physicist Luis Alvarez and his geologist son Walter studied a thin layer of clay found around the world at the end of the Cretaceous. It was rich in iridium, a metal rare on Earth but more abundant in meteorites. Their idea: a huge asteroid impact. It was controversial at first. Then there's the crater, Chicxulub, centred on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula and the same age as the extinction. Today it's the most widely accepted explanation.

cards.fact: The asteroid was about 10 to 15 km wide.
cards.context: It hit so hard it vaporised, throwing debris and soot into the sky. Less sunlight meant less plant growth, and the damage climbed Level 7's food chain: fewer plants, then starving herbivores, then hungry carnivores. Volcanic eruptions in India were already stressing life, but the asteroid was the final blow.

mascot.line: One bad afternoon for the dinosaurs, a very long one for the food chain.

options.label: End-Triassic
options.rationale: The dinosaurs came through this one.

questions.explanation: The end-Permian extinction, about 252 million years ago, took about 90 percent of species.

questions.prompt: What first pointed Luis and Walter Alvarez toward an asteroid impact?

options.label: A sudden fall in sea level
A worldwide clay layer rich in iridium
A meteorite found inside a skeleton

questions.explanation: Iridium is rare on Earth but more abundant in meteorites, so a worldwide iridium-rich layer suggested an impact.

questions.prompt: Using Level 7's food chain, why did the asteroid's soot doom meat-eaters far from the crater?

options.label: Soot poisoned meat but not plants
options.rationale: The harm ran through the plants.

options.label: Carnivores cannot hunt in the dark
options.rationale: The problem was food, not hunting light.

options.label: The blast reached every continent
options.rationale: Distant effects came through the food chain.

options.label: Fewer plants meant fewer herbivores to eat

questions.explanation: Less sunlight cut plant growth; herbivores that eat producers starved, and so did the carnivores that eat them.
